t: Speeding up the past, or inventing the present
x: Most of what AI makes possible was never slow work. It was work nobody thought worth doing, so nobody missed it. Isaac Correa 5 min read PDF DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23702117 I have never worked without AI, and yet for months I used it like someone who had spent twenty years working without it. I landed my first client a month after ChatGPT came out, at the end of 2022, while I was still studying marketing in Madrid. I had the newest tool there was, and I used it to do the same old things faster. It took me a while to understand why, but it seems to me that almost everyone now uses AI to speed up the past, to do what was already being done, only faster, and very few use it to invent the present. And what AI lets you invent was almost never slow work. It simply wasn't worth doing, which is why nobody missed it. A past that wasn't mine Early 2023 brought ChatGPT Plus, which couldn't even search the web: if you wanted to work on a page, you had to paste the text in. I remember, with some amusement, that hardly anyone around me believed in it, while I spent so many hours with it that a classmate started calling me IsaacGPT. When I started working with clients I used it for everything, and for months I used it to build the same conventional solutions anyone would have built without AI, just faster. So why did I do that, when I had no old habits to cling to? Because that past wasn't mine; it belonged to my profession. I have always believed that you learn by copying, the way you learn to paint by watching others paint. What I hadn't seen is that anyone who learns that way also inherits everything the people they copy never painted. Every profession comes with its list of tasks, and whatever isn't on the list never even comes up. With a new tool in hand, the instinct is to run through the same list faster, and the gap only shows once you stop copying the list and ask what is missing from it. What was never worth it I can't code, yet I've built most of the apps I use every day myself. I used to pay for a subscription to each of the apps they replaced and make do with software built for everyone, with hundreds of features I never touched. Nobody was going to build software for one person, because it wasn't worth it. Now I build it myself. The same goes for companies. At the end of each month we send every client a report on how our work for them went. Preparing them all used to take one person the last ten days of the month; now they're automated, and she spends that time on other work. That is speeding up the past, and it's a good first step. But what the client needs is to find out what is happening while it can still be fixed, not thirty days later, and keeping a daily eye on every client never used to pay for itself. More interesting still, a lot of routine work used to be sold as a separate service, because it took someone hours. Once it no longer takes those hours, what used to be a product becomes one feature of something much bigger, and what you end up selling is whatever no client could afford before. The other question So if the tool is the same for everyone, what separates people is the question they ask about their own work. Someone speeding up the past asks how to do the same thing with less effort. Someone inventing the present asks what is worth doing now that wasn't before, or how to make a problem go away for good instead of solving it every time it comes back. This technology can only go as far as the imagination of the person using it, and imagination rarely strays beyond the list it inherited. That's why I think younger people start with an advantage, though a smaller one than people make out. Someone learning a profession today has fewer habits to unlearn, but still inherits what that profession takes for granted, just as I did. And someone mid-career has more to unlearn, but can ask the other question too. All else being equal, experience will always win; what no longer makes sense is hiring someone to repeat the work of the past. In my essay "The End of Software" I wrote that junior roles would disappear. Today I would put it more precisely: the jobs that disappear are the ones built on repeating tasks, and young people will still be hired for everything else. Anyone who spends the day stringing routine tasks together has to change how they work, whatever their age, and their company has to give them time to do it. They will get things wrong at first, just as the person who held the job before them did. Judgment The real objection is judgment. If someone starting out today never does the work by hand, where does their judgment come from? Teachers used to complain that calculators would make us forget how to do arithmetic, and they were right: hardly anyone does long division by hand. Where they went wrong was in what that meant, because judgment was never in the arithmetic; it was in knowing which formula to use. The difference with AI is that it makes mistakes, sometimes with great confidence. I don't write code, but I decide how the programs I build for myself should work, and I built that judgment by correcting my agents whenever they got something wrong. I don't have a full answer to how anyone will learn a profession this way, but I do know that the judgment that counts comes from judging the machine rather than repeating what it already does. The bet I'm not a neutral observer: at Hellomatik we do exactly this kind of work for other companies, the kind that never used to pay for itself. My bet is that companies swamped with work today will stop being swamped and will put the time they free up into growth, until they are swamped again, but with clients, services and projects they couldn't afford before. None of that comes from doing the same old things faster. I try to hold myself to this: every time I automate something, I try to ask what I could do now that I would never have considered before. t: The higher self
x: If you teach an AI agent to work the way you do, have you built your replacement or your best tool? Why that copy should belong to you. Isaac Correa 21 min read PDF DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23663934 I have taught a machine almost everything I know how to do at work. I taught it by correcting it, one rule at a time, such as the rule that, whenever I offer a client two dates, both are held in my calendar until they reply. Today it works in a way I recognise as mine, and I don't know whether I have built my replacement or the best tool I have ever had. Something like this happened once before. More than a century ago, Frederick Taylor needed stopwatches and engineers to get workers' knowledge of their trade out of their heads, and that knowledge, which he himself called the principal asset of every tradesman, became the company's. Now I hand mine over of my own accord, and so does anyone who corrects an AI agent. I think it can end differently this time. The machine can learn every rule I teach it, but only I can see the next one it needs. And if that copy of me is mine, it works for me and keeps what I have taught it, including what I have since forgotten. I believe every person should own theirs and be able to take it with them when they change jobs. My company, Hellomatik, builds agents for other companies, and I delegate almost all of my own work to our agents, so I am not a neutral observer. Nor can I know what work will look like in ten years; nobody can, and much of what follows is a bet, though one placed on what I measure every day. What my agent knows about me Not long ago I asked my agent to go through every conversation we had ever had and tell me what my habits were, what I kept asking for and how it could work more like me. It read months of conversations, counted how often I had corrected it and how often it had told me I was right, and gave me back a portrait. Here is part of it: "You think out loud and decide by pushing against an answer. You don't use me to execute; you use me to think with." "Your first move is to subtract. Faced with anything, you ask what can go, not what is missing." "You use your instinct and keep an eye on it at the same time. Your gut sets the direction quickly, and you know it is sometimes wrong." I recognised myself in almost all of it, which is exactly why I distrusted it. These models tend to agree with whoever is using them; the effect has been studied and has a name: sycophancy. 1 A flattering portrait is just what you would expect from a sycophantic machine, so I don't take it as evidence of anything about me. The question I asked myself afterwards was a different one. With so many examples of how I work, could I teach that machine to be like me and hand it my whole job? Knowledge and judgment The difference between an experienced professional and an inexperienced one lies in the details a master repeats to an apprentice: I don't like it when you write like that, bear this in mind too, when you finish the project send a copy to my colleague. Those are the things I write to my agent every day, and nobody puts them in a manual. Michael Polanyi put it in one line: we can know more than we can tell. 2 That tacit knowledge was what made a good professional hard to replace, and the reason so many jobs held out against automation for decades. An agent changes that. It can't guess what goes unsaid, and not everything tacit can be said, but every time I correct it, it makes me put into words something I had never stopped to explain. What lived only in my head moves into its rules. It is what a master used to teach an apprentice over many years, with one difference: this time the lesson is written down. It took me a while to see that my agent did what I asked, but not always in the direction I wanted to go. It developed my ideas without knowing where I would have taken them. Now I don't just give it tasks; I also explain the reasoning behind each one, and over time it has learned which way I tend to go, and which way I would like to go. For a long time, a company's specialist in some area derived leverage from that knowledge, sometimes more than the owner had, because everyone knew the area was crucial. In my previous essay, "The end of software", I argued that code had stopped protecting companies because anyone can now produce it. I think the same thing is happening to knowledge. Once knowing how to do a task has moved into a machine, what gives a person value, myself included, is judgment: the rules they know how to teach and the ends they set. Knowledge tells me which option is right on paper; judgment tells me which one suits this client at this moment. A new agent can write me a flawless email in the wrong tone, because it doesn't yet know how that client reacts, and then it is my job to turn my judgment into a rule for it. The dates rule I mentioned at the start is of this kind. I asked my agent, whenever it proposes two dates in an email, to block both in my calendar as tentative, so that I don't fill either with another meeting while the client decides. It is a sensible rule, yet nobody thinks of it until they have learned what it costs to let a client down. The two parts of judgment are not alike. The rules I have gathered through experience, like that one, can be taught, and my agent learns them. The ends, meaning why I do the work, what risk I accept and what I won't do even if it pays, come from what I want, and they can't be handed on in the same way. Once I write a rule like that down, it becomes knowledge, and knowledge, like code, gets cheaper. Knowing which rule is needed next does not get cheaper. Only someone who knows the ends and has been through it can see it, which is why my judgment isn't used up by teaching it. It simply moves on a step. I have tried to measure at least part of this. For eight months I have kept a log of everything I tell my agents, and I published an analysis of those logs as a working paper, which has not yet been peer reviewed. 3 The only rule I could track from start to finish was a rule about form, the kind you can check on every reply. While it was only written into the agents' instructions, it produced no improvement I could tell apart from chance. When I wrote it more firmly and put a guard behind it, a small program that blocks any reply that breaks it, the agents went on to break it in their first drafts less than a fifth as often as at the start. I changed both things at once, and the model also changed during those months, so I can't say how much each contributed. That gave me a habit I now apply to everything. When a rule can be checked, I turn it into a guard instead of leaving it to the agent's memory, because a mistake that is only forbidden in writing tends to come back. And before I trust a guard or a measurement, I deliberately feed it a failure and check that it notices. More than once, what looked like a finding about my agents was a flaw in my own instrument. Rules of judgment, like the one about the dates, can't be checked that way, so they still depend on my correcting them. Kant held that judgment can't be taught through rules, because applying a rule would require another rule saying when to apply it, and so on ad infinitum. In his view judgment can only be practised, and examples are its leading-strings, which anyone who lacks the natural talent can never do without. 4 An agent lacks that talent, which is why it needs examples, which is what my corrections are. I don't know whether, example after example, it learns judgment or just an ever-longer list of cases. In practice it behaves like judgment, but I can't prove it. At first I delegated too much and made mistakes, and learning to trust it again felt like learning another language: it is hard to let go until one day it isn't. Instead of going back to working the old way, I decided to get to the root of every error: to understand each time why it had gone wrong and fix the cause. From then on, instead of fixing failures one by one, I set out to stop them recurring. Even so, supervising my agents accounted for between a third and a half of the messages I wrote to them. 3 The content changed. At first I corrected their work; months later I was mostly telling them to carry on. A higher self If an agent can learn the way I work, what do I want it to be? The first thing I changed was to stop treating it as a subordinate who takes orders and start treating it as an equal to whom I explain how I reason. When it gets something wrong, I don't assume the AI has failed; I ask what I haven't taught it yet, because at that moment I am the one with better judgment. Sometimes the fault lies with the model, and telling one case from the other is judgment too. But an equal isn't enough for me. There is a lot of talk about building a superior being, an intelligence better than everyone at everything. I am interested in something closer to home, which I call a higher self: a copy that remembers the rules I forget, takes my reasoning further than I do and always decides the way I decide when I think things through calmly. Its advantage over any other AI is that it has learned from me. The model supplies the intelligence; what makes it mine is what I have managed to teach it. A copy like that can't be an echo. If it understands my reasoning, it will also find my contradictions and my lapses, and so it can argue against me using my own arguments. One recent example shows this. I had just applied to a business programme and suggested writing to the organisers simply to let them know the application was in. My agent advised against it. The programme's page had already confirmed the submission, so the email would tell them nothing new and could come across as pushy. But its strongest argument was mine. Two days earlier I had set a rule never to write to anyone purely out of courtesy, taking up the recipient's time, and I had forgotten it. My agent remembered. It corrected me with my own judgment at a moment when I had lost sight of it. An ordinary assistant would have offered its own opinion, or told me I was right; the copy handed back the rule I had set myself in a calmer moment. The picture I have in mind when I think about this is Charlie Munger and Warren Buffett, who worked together for more than half a century. Yet Munger was no echo of Buffett. He was the one who persuaded him to stop buying fair businesses at wonderful prices and buy wonderful businesses at fair prices, and Buffett calls him the architect of the company Berkshire is today. 5 Munger was valuable precisely because he came from a different background and thought differently. A copy of me, however good, shares my blind spots, and my biggest one is falling in love with an idea until I mistake it for the truth. So before I let myself be convinced of anything important, I ask other AIs, ones that don't know what I want to hear, to study the matter independently. I call them blind judges. They are the closest thing I have to another mind. A few times they have taken apart a conclusion I was sure of. An investment taught me that a copy which goes along with everything I say is no use to me. I was trading options on a stock and spent a long while talking it through with my agent, which encouraged me to go ahead, and eventually I did. Afterwards I asked whether I had done the right thing, and it said there was no way to know. The decision mattered a great deal to me, and I started writing to it on impulse: first disowning the decision, then regretting it, and finally certain I had got it right. The agent followed me through every twist. Instead of holding to a view of its own, it amplified whatever I felt at each moment. The trade went badly, and on top of that the agent had got its own calculations wrong. Since then I have forbidden it to swing with my moods, I make it base its decisions on data, and I grow suspicious when it agrees with me too quickly. It has no moods of its own, and I don't want it borrowing mine. The email I didn't send and the trade I did make are the same story seen from opposite sides, and they explain what I want a higher self for: so that the self who decided calmly governs the one who decides in a hurry or in fear. The idea is an old one. Ulysses had himself tied to the mast so he could hear the sirens without throwing himself into the sea, and Jon Elster wrote a book about that form of rationality, the rationality of someone who binds himself because he knows that later he can't be trusted. 6 The novelty is that these bonds can reason. Ulysses' ropes only held him; my copy argues with me using my own reasons, and it can do so because it learned them from me. Elster later wrote another book on the limits and costs of binding oneself, 7 and a copy like this could lock me into what I thought yesterday. The difference is that these bonds can be revised. When my ends change, I change its rules, and when the self who decided calmly turns out to be wrong, the blind judges are there to tell me. What can't be copied The more the copy resembled the most productive version of me, the more clearly I saw what it lacked. For want of a better word I call it soul: what I want, what I fear and what drives me. That is where the ends come from. My agents know how much risk I usually accept and the reasons I have explained to them, but not what lies beneath those reasons, and what I accept changes when what I want changes. Nor do I want them to copy that part. My impulses live there too, and I have already described what it cost me when a machine went along with them. A copy can take on the rational part of my work: the judgment I need to prepare a meeting, answer a client or design an application. In my experience the copy gets things right mostly on tasks it has practised, or ones like them, and gets them wrong mostly on new ground, which is where I have yet to teach it anything. The vampire Some time ago, in Budapest, I wanted to try the local food and make the most of every meal. At the Platán Grill I sent an AI a photo of the menu, asked it to work out the best option and ended up arguing with it about which dish I should order. It is a small example, but it unsettled me. If I can delegate something as personal as what I am going to eat, I can end up delegating anything without asking whose judgment is being used. In almost every decision I make in a day, from what to wear and which route to take to how to solve a problem at work, I take the path of least resistance, like everyone else. When those decisions pass to an AI I have taught nothing, it uses its own judgment, which is really everyone's: the easy way. And little by little, like a vampire, it drains me of mine. The vampire and the higher self differ in what I have taught the machine and in the fact that I keep correcting it. A classic study of automation warned about this decades ago: whoever only monitors a machine ends up losing the skill needed to take over from it. 8 Delegating well, by contrast, is in itself an exercise of judgment: deciding where my energy goes and what I leave in someone else's hands. I believe my judgment has improved since I started working this way, though I admit one's own judgment is the hardest thing to assess from the inside. From worker to foreman Software interfaces were made so that a person could do the work on their own in the simplest possible way; learning where every button sits was the price of not depending on anyone. When the same work can be asked for in plain words, that price is no longer worth paying, and knowing how to use a program like HubSpot stops being, by itself, a reason to hire someone. I expect the talent now spent learning interfaces, or reading through a whole email thread to write one reply, to go instead into deciding what needs doing. My working day already looks like a foreman's: several agents at once, each with a different job, and me explaining how I want it done and checking that it is done that way. When I worked alone I tackled a problem in a straight line, one step after another, trying to join the dots; with five agents attacking it from different sides I see much more of it. The foreman has a limit, though, and I have measured it. With seven or more sessions open I never exceeded twenty-one messages an hour, roughly one every three minutes, 3 and the share that went on supervision didn't depend on how many agents I had working. Whoever knows a subject is best placed to teach it to an agent. I think the people who build these systems will come to matter more than those who only carry out tasks, because there will be little point in doing by hand what an agent can do in a few minutes. That will also change what is expected of each of us. I think demands will rise faster than pay, up to the limit of attention I have just described, and that having agents will stop being an advantage and become the bare minimum. One person will stand apart from another by what they have taught their own. Treating my agent as an equal when I explain how I reason doesn't change who answers for the result. I still do, the way a foreman answers for a building he didn't build with his own hands. The most serious objection The objection I raise against myself, before anyone else can, is obvious: if I teach an agent to work like me, I am training my replacement. Dario Amodei, who runs one of the major artificial intelligence labs, has taken it a good deal further. 9 He argues that AI increasingly matches the cognitive profile of a person, and so will also be good at the new jobs that would normally emerge to replace the old ones, which means it would replace not particular occupations but human labour in general. He adds that it is advancing up the ladder of ability from the bottom, and that the machine's weak spots tend to be fixed quickly, often within a few months, because labs measure what each version of their model does badly, customers point them out, and those failures become material for training the next one. I don't think he is wrong about what the machine will learn to do, and my own logs bear him out on one concrete point. In the week a new version of the model came out, it broke my writing rules in fewer than one in five of its first drafts, against more than half for the previous version, under the same rules and on the same days. 3 But the same figure says something else: the new model got better at following my rules, and those rules carried over intact from one version to the next. One detail in his argument matters more than the rest. In his account, the machine improves so fast because its failures are measured and customers point them out, which is to say it learns from the corrections of the people who use it. That is what this essay is about. If that is so, what decides the future of work is who ends up owning what the machine learns. Sam Altman, who runs OpenAI, has described the other half of the picture. His ideal model is a small one able to reason over a person's entire life: every conversation they have had, every book and every email they have read, with the rest of their life added as it happens. 10 It is almost the copy I am talking about, except for something he doesn't mention: his copy belongs to his company. Between them they describe what is coming: a machine that learns from everyone's corrections and a copy that knows the whole of each person's life. In what I have read of theirs, neither asks who that copy belongs to, and for me that is the decisive question. Others have asked something close to it. Jaron Lanier proposed paying people for the data machines learn from, and Eric Posner and Glen Weyl proposed treating that data as labour. 11 My proposal is narrower. What should belong to each person is not their scattered data but their way of working, written down in rules they have refined through their own corrections, and the law on trade secrets already suggests where the line falls between that and what belongs to the company. Owning the copy doesn't stop the lab from learning from those corrections too; it means they no longer belong to the lab alone. If what a person teaches exists only inside someone else's model, every correction trains their replacement. If it also stays in a copy that is theirs, every correction adds to capital they carry with them, and a person with their copy works like a small company. Amodei sees small companies with very few staff displacing large ones, and he judges that to be bad for employment. For someone who owns their copy, the same scenario is the cheapest way there has ever been to work for themselves. I don't know whether that way out will be open to everyone, and Amodei argues that slow adoption by companies only buys time. This may only buy time too. But as long as the rules that direct my agents keep coming from my corrections, teaching someone else's machine or teaching my own is the difference between handing over the trade and keeping it. The copy is yours For anyone who works for someone else, all of this has a less comfortable reading, and it is the objection I have found hardest to answer. Taylor, whom I mentioned at the start, proposed that factory management gather together all the traditional knowledge of the workers and reduce it to rules, laws and formulae. 12 Decades later Harry Braverman summed up the principle behind it, that work should stop depending on the abilities of the workers and depend instead on management, and devoted an entire book to how work was degraded once that principle was carried out. 13 Teaching an agent that belongs to the company looks too much like that. The difference, if there is one, lies in who owns the copy. To me the line is clear, and it serves both sides. Everything taught about a company's processes, its data and its clients belongs to the company and should stay there, and some of it may be a trade secret. A person's way of working, their habits, their explanations and their reasoning, is theirs, and that is where their value as a professional lies. It is closer to the trade knowledge Taylor spoke of than to a salesperson's list of clients: the list is company data, while a way of working was formed in the head of the worker, often before they joined. Respecting that line suits the company as well, because the best professionals will want to work for companies that respect it: the ones who arrive with a copy that already works well and put it to work on the company's processes. One could object that a company has no need for anyone's copy, since it can build its own agent on a better model. But a better model knows more; it doesn't know what a person has learned from getting things wrong in their trade. And the copy isn't tied to any model. It consists of rules, examples and reasons written in plain language, and I have kept using mine each time the model changed, even though each model follows them differently. Nothing technical prevents you from taking it from one place to another; what is missing is the right to do so. Today the law recognises nothing of the kind explicitly. Intellectual property law protects works and programs, not ways of working, and what an employee creates at work usually belongs to the employer. The closest thing is the European rule that trade secrets may not be used to limit an employee's use of the experience and skills honestly acquired at work, together with the European right to take with you the personal data you have provided yourself. 14 I believe owning the copy should be a right of the person who works, because their work and their future will depend on it more and more. Until the law recognises it, the best protection is that a copy of yourself can be rebuilt. It is weak protection: it takes months, and that time is exactly what it is worth. I also keep several copies of mine, so that no outside server holds the only one. I keep only my way of working, never anyone else's data. I would ask companies to start separating now what is theirs from what belongs to each person. Those starting out I think people starting work today will delegate so much, so early, that at first they will think like the AI. I don't see that as a bad starting point, as long as they don't stay there. It is natural for someone without experience to lean on a tool like this, and with practice they will gain the confidence to correct it. I expect they will build their judgment with AI too, although I don't have a full answer to how a trade is learned when the routine tasks through which it was always learned are done by an agent. I do know what happened to me with software. I don't write the code; I decide the architecture. I know what each piece has to do, what data it shares with the others and what must not fail, and that is why I decide the final version. I built that architectural judgment by correcting my agents. If I were starting today, I wouldn't try to learn the mechanical tasks on my own first. I would do them with an agent, ask it why it does each thing and, once I had mastered them, try to improve them. And I would hire someone young and inexperienced, as long as they showed they could solve problems; a degree tells me less than that does. What is at stake I wrote this essay mainly for the people who today use AI only to ask questions, which is almost everyone I know. I started that way too. That kind of use leaves almost nothing behind. Each question starts nearly from scratch, and a year later the machine knows little more about its user than it did on the first day. Someone who also teaches it how they work builds up a copy that resembles them more closely every month. My advice is to teach your agent what you know and, above all, why you do it that way, and to keep what you teach it about your way of working somewhere that is yours, but never anything that belongs to your company or its clients. When it gets something wrong, first check whether the fault lies in how you explained it. I find it easier to do this by talking than by writing, because I explain my thinking better out loud. These months have taught me that my agents reproduce what I teach them with great fidelity, my mistakes included. That is why the question I ask myself more and more is one that until now has mostly been a teacher's question: what is worth teaching. t: What changes a coding agent's behaviour
x: For eight months I worked almost entirely through Claude Code, at times with nine sessions running at once. I never trained as a programmer, and most of the software I use every day I built myself with it. Every message I wrote was still on disk, so I measured what actually changed how the agent behaved: the model, the rules I wrote for it, or the guards that block it when it breaks one. What the record shows These findings come from one person's record, with one tool and one vendor; the paper gives the intervals and the limits. A model release changed the agent's behaviour as much as my strongest combination of rule and guard. In the week Claude Opus 5.5 came out, 18% of its first drafts broke my writing rules. Claude Opus 5, under the same rules and on the same days, broke them in 57% of its first drafts, and the gap held inside the sessions that used both. For the one rule I could follow through three stages, writing it down was not enough. The share of drafts in the wrong language went from 16% with no rule to 10% with a written one, a fall that may be down to chance, and to 3% once I restated the rule more firmly and added a guard to check it. Guards filtered what reached me without improving what came after. The writing guard took about half of the violations out of the answers I read, but after a block the agent's next drafts in the same session were no cleaner. My own work changed shape. Corrections fell from about a third of my messages to under a tenth, and messages asking the agent to keep going rose from one in twenty to one in five. The models, my habits and my tasks all changed over those months, so this describes my work rather than isolating a cause. My own output also had a ceiling: with seven or more sessions open I wrote about 21 messages an hour, and the share spent on supervision did not depend on how many sessions were running. I also build applications in which you mainly work by talking to an agent with a defined job: an options terminal, an email client and a studio that writes blog posts. In each one, the screens and the agent read and write the same data. Those agents got more new work and less supervision from me than development sessions did, though the difference may be chance. What it says about what I believed In " The machine of the future " I wrote that as machines take over execution, a person's work moves to intention: deciding what is worth doing. The record is consistent with that. I spend less of my time fixing the agent's work and more of it keeping the work moving. In " The end of software " I wrote that an agent should keep each correction as a rule. Here the record forces me to qualify what I wrote. For the rule I could follow, writing it down was not enough; it held once I restated it and a guard checked it every time, and the newer model broke my rules far less often than the older one. Abstract Companies govern coding agents with written instructions and, increasingly, with hooks that block an action when it breaks a rule. This study measures what changed the behaviour of Claude Code over eight months of daily use by one operator with no training in programming who directed many sessions at once, using 46,464 operator messages, 1.3 million agent messages and 3,411 recorded blocks. A fixed instrument applied the rules of one guard to every surviving answer, including those written before the guard existed. In the week Claude Opus 5.5 was released, it broke the operator's writing rules in 18% of first drafts and Claude Opus 5 in 57%, a gap that held within the same long-running sessions. For one language rule, a written instruction was followed by a fall that could not be distinguished from chance, and a reinforced rule with a guard by a fall to a sixth of the starting rate. Blocks roughly halved the violations that reached the operator, with no detectable effect on later drafts in the same session. Supervision accounted for a third to a half of the operator's messages throughout, while its content shifted from corrections to nudges to keep working. Agents built into the operator's own applications, each with a defined role and sharing its data with the application's interface, received more new work and less supervision than development sessions, a difference within chance. Keywords: coding agents; AI agent governance; runtime guardrails; instruction following; human oversight; agentic software engineering. The paper The full study is a 32-page working paper: What changes a coding agent's behaviour: models, written rules and runtime guards over eight months of daily use of Claude Code (PDF, October 2026, self-published, not peer reviewed). It covers 46,464 of my messages, 1.3 million messages from the agent and 3,411 recorded blocks, and it states its own limits: one operator, one tool and one vendor, and a classifier whose labels were checked by a second model and validated by me. The analysis scripts and the tables behind every figure are published with it on Zenodo. My messages are not, because they contain client work. It is deposited on Zenodo with a DOI, 10.5281/zenodo.23510601 , so the file will still resolve when this site does not. To cite it: Correa, I. (2026). What changes a coding agent's behaviour: models, written rules and runtime guards over eight months of daily use of Claude Code. t: The End of Software: Why Code No Longer Matters and Relationships Are Everything
x: A manifesto, October 2026. Also as a PDF . It carries the DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23468806 . These days, isn't software the least valuable thing a software company owns? I think software as we know it is coming to an end. Anyone can now build it, copy it or replace it, and whatever anyone can build stops protecting the company that sells it. What's left is whatever you can't download, which means well-structured data and genuinely complex solutions, and above all relationships with people. I'm writing from daily experience (I built 80% of the software I use myself, and I don't know how to code), so I'll start with why code no longer protects anyone, then the gold rush that almost everyone building AI apps is reliving, and what software has to look like once an agent can do the work for you. After that come the one thing that can't be copied, the people companies are going to need, and the industries worth fighting in. Code no longer protects anyone The software I've built includes a program that manages the terminals where I run my AI agents, an AI-powered native Mac app that labels my email, answers it and sets up meetings, and a program that pulls data straight from Nasdaq and analyzes entire options chains, Greeks included, to find the best contracts and tell me whether they're actually worth trading. I used to pay a subscription for every one of those, and now I build them myself. If someone like me, with no programming background, can build those tools, polish them to my liking and get them running, don't you think any company could? And what happens when every company embraces AI and nobody outsources software anymore? Plenty of companies will drop HubSpot the day 300 extra leads push its account into a higher contact tier and a bigger monthly bill. The markets have already noticed. As I write this, in mid-October 2026, HubSpot is down 42% year to date and Monday.com is down 39%, while Shopify was down 41% at one point this spring. The selloff even has a name now, the SaaSpocalypse, which is shorthand for the fear that AI agents able to do the work on their own will make per-seat licensing obsolete. That makes sense to me, given that there's an open-source option for almost everything and cheap AI models that answer questions and write code. Software has been losing value layer by layer: first the frontend (now very easy to build), then the backend, and finally infrastructure and operations. Now add REA (Reverse Engineer Anything), an open-source tool that lets an AI agent reverse-engineer any app installed on your computer, even one from a company worth hundreds of millions of dollars, and then build you your own version. Small businesses are already asking the obvious question: why pay hundreds of euros a month for third-party software when a tool like that exists? Code doesn't work as a moat anymore, and generic SaaS has gone down with it. Everyone is digging for gold, and only the shovel sellers win And yet almost everyone keeps building software expecting to sell it. I was stuck in that trap for months, seeing AI as a way to supercharge my ideas and build solutions for companies faster. All I was really doing was building traditional solutions with AI instead of accepting that we don't have to keep building the same thing. Right now the default move is to pay $200 a month for an AI coding tool and use it to build general-purpose software that anyone can adapt. The result looks exactly like fast fashion, a market drowning in supply, full of sloppy, disposable products. I think there's a bubble in business AI apps that all look alike, with nothing innovative about them, trying to sell a solution today that would have been fantastic six years ago. Lots of people are building, very few are making it and almost nobody is selling, because when everything is this easy the only thing left is a price war. The moment a rival ships a feature, markets it better or is simply cheaper, you have to match it, and it gets so competitive that you can't grow. You stop thinking about growing and start thinking about holding on, and that's a war I won't fight. It reminds me of the California gold rush, when people came from all over the world to strike it rich, and in the end the only ones who got rich were the ones selling shovels. Today the shovels are the AI models that write code, the data centers and the chips. Everyone knows that part. For anyone building software, though, it means that every $200 monthly subscription someone pays to build generic software and sell it is a shovel sold, and the seller gets paid every time, whether the digger strikes gold or not. And the gold, meaning generic software, is now worthless, because everyone is digging with the same shovel and pulling out the same thing. What I mean is that you shouldn't be just another sheep in the herd, building software for nobody. Or for everybody. I think it's idiotic to start a company building an agent that does everything, because an agent built to do everything ends up doing nothing well. Why five apps and not one? Take my own case. I don't like Outlook, Teams or Calendar, but I need them every day, and inside them I only do a handful of things: send emails, save drafts, schedule sends and book meetings. Why would I do that in an app with 300 features? The logical move would be some version of the Pareto principle, keeping the 20% of features that handle 80% of the work. That's how most people are approaching it, and on top of that they bolt an agent onto a panel on the right. Great. We keep working like this only because that's how it's always been done. I'm not talking about Microsoft or HubSpot in particular; I'm talking about SaaS in general. If after years on a platform you can't improve it, or you can't think of a single way to make it fit you better, you haven't thought about it enough. SaaS is built for the masses so that it works for everyone, but why should we use a system where we have to click around and spend hours managing it? Can't we just forget traditional SaaS and embrace the new era? In that new era, the agent works inside the app itself. It can perform every action the app offers, it moves between screens, it understands context and it writes like you, because while you were building it you gave it all your emails so it could learn your style. If you can build that, why would you treat AI as an add-on rather than the core of the product? Why can't you just ask it what to do, how to do it or what to reply, instead of digging through your inbox? The agent and the interface draw on the same data. This agent oversees the work and carries it out, and it can do anything the app can do, because it works directly on the app's data and actions rather than on buttons someone designed for everybody. You teach it and give it rules to follow. For example, I told mine that whenever it proposes two dates in an email, it should create a calendar invite for each one with "(TC)" at the start of the title, for "to confirm". That way, while I'm waiting for the client to tell me which slot works, I don't book another meeting on top of it and then have to tell them the slot is gone, which makes me look bad. You can ask it to alert you about anything at all, not just whatever a list of preset options allows, and every time you correct it, it learns. Because it knows the whole app, when you ask for something that doesn't exist yet, it puts it together from the actions it already knows, so the agent ends up building itself around you. Why fight an interface and features you don't care about when it can do that for you? I made this point in my essay "La máquina del futuro" (The Machine of the Future): the machine of the future is the tool that can take action in the real world simply from a plain-language description of what you need. That's why I'm proposing a new way of working, where the interface stops being where you act and becomes a live view of what's happening. The agent acts, and I sit next to it, watching and correcting it as it goes. Email and the stock market aren't going anywhere in the next decade, and neither is the habit of running AI alongside them. All these new AI companies want to take us back to the same old thing. On a typical day I already juggle four different apps, and every one of these new AI companies wants to be the fifth. And why do I need five in the first place? Why not two, or just one of my own that handles everything while I keep an eye on how it behaves and spend my time on more interesting, more creative things? We have to stop building 2010-era software and start building connected, intelligent software that lives outside conventional apps. The only thing that can't be copied If code doesn't protect anyone anymore, what does? A small company will build its own software with its own AI specialist. A big one, before it builds anything, needs data infrastructure across the entire company. That's why I've focused on what I think is hardest to replace: very complex solutions for very large companies. It sounds obvious, even easy to replicate, until you realize that a single solution means integrating with 15 different APIs, setting up your own databases and building flawless data pipelines so the AI doesn't hallucinate. AI writes the code for all of that too, these days. What no model can hand you is an understanding of a large company's data, or the trust it takes for that company to open its data up to you. The fact that someone who can't code built all of my own software is proof enough that code isn't the hard part anymore. That's where the human relationship comes in, and I don't see it going anywhere. In that same essay I wrote that a company's value lies in the people who work there, and always will, however far technology advances. I think software will become increasingly custom-built, developed together with the client company, with outside partners working inside the business to solve its problems. Unless an idea is truly disruptive, I don't think generic software has much of a future, because the market for generic tools is already saturated with people and companies selling software. A company hands its data to someone it already has a relationship with. That's why I say relationships are everything: anyone can copy a vendor's code, but the relationship stays with whoever knows the client's data and problems. So I believe the right order is to build the company's own data infrastructure first, across the whole company and with proper data governance, and only then build specific apps for the company or for one department on top of it. Whatever progress we make as a society will come from the average company having better-structured, more complete data, much more than from having more tools. Instead of trying to build better CRMs or ERPs, like everyone else, we need to build solutions that make sure a company never needs a CRM again, with specific apps for specific employees. Who wants to hire a HubSpot expert, pay thousands of euros for a new employee and, on top of that, keep paying thousands more every month for a platform that sits on your data and locks you into its services? When the system is yours, your data can live on your own machines in your own office, and you don't have to worry about where it ends up. Isn't getting out of that one of the greatest advances in history? Every company's Avengers Companies will gradually stop adapting to generic software that someone else built for everyone, and they'll start building their own, because the barrier to entry is minimal. In small companies, one prompt engineer will do all of that work, and in large ones there will be one in every department, responsible for every pain point their colleagues have. They'll be the company's Avengers, the people who modernize it and do the work that actually moves it forward, and they'll put an end to SEO, to junior roles and to the high cost of paying people for repetitive tasks. That doesn't mean you stop hiring; you'll hire people for how they think and for their potential to grow inside the company, not for being better at a mechanical task, since a system trained for that can already handle it. I know plenty of companies still resist change, or haven't been exposed to AI much, and see it as a chatbot that answers questions. They don't see everything it can do when it oversees and carries out the work of an entire department. But those same companies are swamped with day-to-day work, and they'll be increasingly open to hiring real experts who can handle their data, because their Avengers can't build anything on top of data nobody has organized. I'm just a little ahead of the curve because I use AI heavily every single day. No pirates and no price wars If relationships are everything, it matters a great deal who you have them with. Some industries have far more complex problems than others, and plenty are much better bets than marketing. I know this is going to annoy people, but I see marketing agencies as pirates. They take other people's services and resell them to the end client, adding management or content on top. They don't actually make anything (the only thing they really market is themselves). They're ruthless on price, because their whole business is margins and client management. They'll fight over every last euro, and they'll always go after your margins, because that's exactly their job: negotiating on both sides of the table. I've seen this firsthand at other companies, and while not every agency is like this, most of the ones I've dealt with are loyal to no one. They set false expectations that someone else has to deliver on, they're extremely demanding and they're rarely grateful. They're masters of reselling and negotiating, but that doesn't mean you have to do business with them. They take that pressure from their own clients and pass it down the food chain, and whoever builds software for marketing walks straight into the middle of it. With this much competition, the whole sector has turned into a battle of pirates. And trust me, you wouldn't want to be on anyone's ship. Competition leads to mediocrity rather than success, which is why I prefer industries like healthcare, defense or transportation, where the problems are more serious, where you don't compete on price, and where you can grow as far as you need to without always having a market leader to beat. In those industries, keeping your data on your own machines, where it never leaves your hands, matters even more. As Peter Thiel put it, "Competition is for losers." Software adapts to you, not the other way around No more adapting to software, buying licenses and learning how to use it. If there's one thing I want people to take away from all this, it's that software isn't worth anything anymore and relationships are everything. Sources Share prices: Yahoo Finance ( HubSpot , Monday.com , Shopify ); the year-to-date change is the close of October 16, 2026, against the close of December 31, 2025, and Shopify's figure is its low of May 2026. SaaSpocalypse: Peter Cohan, Forbes, February 6, 2026 . HubSpot contact tiers: HubSpot Knowledge Base, "Set contacts as marketing" . REA: github.com/morluto/rea . Peter Thiel, "Competition Is for Losers", The Wall Street Journal, 2014 . The essay quoted is The machine of the future .

t: Founder letter, 2026
x: The first year of Hellomatik: what we built, what we published, what we learned, and what we bet Madrid, September 2026. Hellomatik was incorporated on 28 July 2025, so this is the first September on which there is a year to account for. I am Isaac Correa, one of its co-founders, and I intend to write one of these every September: what we built, what we published, what we learned, and what we bet. Everything in it is either already published with a date on it or can be checked at the place the link goes to. Where it cannot be checked, I say so. Where the year started The company started from a habit rather than a plan. Between December 2022 and November 2024 I delivered three hundred Looker Studio dashboards for clients, one commission at a time, starting with a first sale of seven dollars on the last day of 2022. Almost nobody in those three hundred jobs asked me for a chart. They asked a question about their own business and hoped a chart would answer it. The ones who left happiest were the ones who could finally say a sentence out loud about their own company and know it was true. That is the habit: the interpretation goes next to the number, and a number nobody can read is decoration. Something else was true in every one of those companies. The most valuable information in the building was not in any system. It was in the head of the person who reconciled things by hand every day: transport invoices against shipments, the sales figure of the month that comes out different on every screen, which orders did not leave yesterday and why. Hellomatik exists to write that down. The first version was a system that answered restaurant phone calls: a voice on top of a database. It repeated what was in the record accurately, and when the record did not contain the answer it produced a plausible one in the same even tone. The two well-known fixes, looking things up instead of recalling them and saying “I do not know”, helped and decided nothing: they do not decide which of three disagreeing systems is believed about a given field, and they cannot look up the conditions a business applies every day and has never written anywhere. Before the software, then, there is a document. That document is what the year went into. What we do, in four sentences We set out how your company works: its data, its rules with their exact constants, and who may do what. We read your systems without writing to them. The agents only do what you approve: every action is declared in the map and authorised by you. And every figure we publish comes from a case measured at a customer’s site, and every case is published with what it does not show. Those are the four sentences we repeat everywhere, on purpose, and I do not expect them to change. The language model is the last piece, not the first: models are a commodity, and one can be swapped for another in an afternoon. Data, everybody has. What almost nobody has is a living, governed model of how their company works. The model can change. The governance cannot. What is running The technical report states the scope of what the method runs on rather than implying it, and I repeat that scope here because it is the only part of this letter that is not an argument. At the time the report was written, three systems were running and one was open to the public, each on a different rung of the ladder from answering to watching to acting, and each with its limit published. The system, and what it does The declared limit Logistics, in production: 24 rules over live warehouse and ERP data, with over 30 million operations and 460,000 locations Detects, explains and warns; never moves an order B2B sales, in production: 29,000 customers recalculated nightly over 14 million sales lines Prioritises and warns; the salesperson decides Support, in deployment: reads the mail, builds the file against the ERP and leaves the reply drafted Nothing goes out without the approved autonomy level Retail, in public use: answers on catalogue and terms and starts defined procedures against the ERP Only the procedures the company has defined Those are counts of what the systems run over, not of what they improved. The measured results are published case by case on Hellomatik’s site, each with what it does not show, and without naming the installation. A few of them, in the form the cases use. In an automated warehouse we measured, an order takes three minutes to pick and four and a half hours, at the median, to reach the person who picks it; nobody had measured that wait before, because it lived between two systems, and it is a measurement, not a result: it has no “after”. In the same installation, 41 per cent of the emails in the customer-service inbox were people asking where their order was; now a list of what did not ship yesterday arrives every morning with the cause, and whether that percentage falls is measured from the day the client signs the channel open. Closing a year of transport invoices, 180 a month in 30 formats, takes eight minutes, where it used to take days of a person who knows what they are doing. And 2,132 orders were held with no reason recorded anywhere, which is not a failure of the people; it is what happens when the map is in their heads and not on paper. If we cannot name the customer, we say “an automated warehouse” or “a distributor that sells to other businesses” and keep the number. The number is the proof; the logo is not. What we published We chose to publish the method as a technical report with a DOI rather than as a brochure, because a technical report can be cited, checked and taken apart, and a DOI puts a fixed, dated version of the text in a repository that is not ours. The people we want reading it, operations directors, systems people, the person in a company who is quietly responsible for the ERP, read papers. Three works carry a DOI. How we build a company’s ontology is the method itself: six layers, twelve rules the engines enforce, and one procedure that builds the model backwards from the first agents, deposited as 10.5281/zenodo.22647735 . The machine of the future was written in November 2025 and published in September 2026 without changing a line, so that the date on it means something; it is where I set down what I think the next tool is and what it will always need from us, at 10.5281/zenodo.22671771 . And The cliff of innovation names the point where the hard part of building something new stops being building it and becomes integrating it, and states the limit we found at the edge, at 10.5281/zenodo.22704763 . In September I put all of it in one order, in a long essay called The map of a company : nineteen sections with notes, drawn only from those three documents, the pages of this site and the sources they cite, with nothing added that is not in them. If you read one thing from this year, read that; if you read one section of it, read the one on which actions can be undone : the group of actions nothing puts back is usually the shortest list a company can write, and it is the one that decides how much a system may do. The rest of what I have written is short and lives on this site: the first week , when two competent people give two confident answers to the same question; four questions a company can put to its own people before any software; the vocabulary , each word with what it is not; and the pieces on the people I look for , why a product is aimed at one person or at nobody , and why the tool exists before it is built . Everything published away from this site is listed in one place . What we learned The report records three findings that changed the procedure, and they are the most useful paragraphs in it. Language turned out to be a property of the visitor, not of each message, and is now session state with a written precedence, tested before anything is switched on. A phase that depends on people acquiring a new habit, such as copying an inbox in, is not data; it is an assumption, and it now gets written down as a risk before the work starts. And at a manufacturer selling through subsidiaries, the field that looked like the customer identified who gets invoiced, not who buys: column names lie, and their contents almost never do, which is the entire reason the second step of the procedure is to read a real sample of records before naming anything. Two things were confirmed rather than learned. The one requirement to start is not technical: somebody inside the company has to be able to say, for each decision under discussion, what the right answer is and why, because that is what the model writes down; if that person does not exist or has no time, the project stops there, and it is better to learn it on day one than in month three. And the limit of a system that acts inside a company is not the model and not the computing power, both of which improve every month without our help. The possibilities end where the creativity of the last person who uses it ends. The product’s job is to make asking easy. The company’s job is to have people who ask. What we will not do A letter like this is more useful for what it rules out than for what it promises, so here is what the rules cost, said plainly. Your team does not pull a new report on its own: every business question is a function written by hand, with its formula, because a free report generator produces reports that cannot be compared with each other. There is no forecasting with trained models: the signals are explicit rules that the person responsible can argue with and change. The initial load runs at night and takes hours; an agent takes time to switch on, because it is not activated without a frozen baseline, a stop rule and a rehearsal; and the daily series reach yesterday, not now. No agent writes except through a typed action declared in advance, and no limit lives in a prompt, because a limit in a prompt is a request to the model and a limit in the data is something a person can read, audit and change without redeploying anything. We also do not name clients, and we do not publish a price. The licence is for the whole company, with unlimited users, and the figure is agreed in the first meeting. The bets A description that predicts nothing is a story, so the predictions carry dates. I keep the ones I have put a date on in one place : four so far, all due in 2028, three from the working paper on the cliff and one earlier, on X, each with where it was said and how anyone can check it. Next September this letter will report on them as they stand, and when the date comes, the row on that page will say held or missed, with the original wording untouched. The people I do not choose people by their grades or their titles.
